results.question: how long do i keep tax records
results.answer:
The IRS requires you to keep tax records for the period that the Internal Revenue Code allows you (or the IRS) to review those records.

**General rule**  
You must keep records as long as they may be needed for the administration of any provision of the Internal Revenue Code.  “Generally, this means you must keep records that support an item of income or deduction on a return until the period of limitations for that return runs out.”  [[1]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/318-irs_publication_583_starting_a_business.pdf#page=16)

**Period‑of‑limitations table**  
The period of limitations is the time in which you can amend your return to claim a credit or refund, or the IRS can assess additional tax.  The table in the publication lists the specific periods for each type of return.  [[1]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/318-irs_publication_583_starting_a_business.pdf#page=16)

**Employment‑tax records**  
If you have employees, you must keep employment‑tax records for **at least 4 years after the date the tax becomes due or is paid, whichever is later**.  [[1]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/318-irs_publication_583_starting_a_business.pdf#page=16)

**Asset‑related records**  
For property (e.g., machinery, equipment), keep records until the period of limitations expires for the year in which you dispose of the property in a taxable disposition.  [[1]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/318-irs_publication_583_starting_a_business.pdf#page=16)

**Other notes**  
- Keep copies of filed tax returns; they help prepare future returns and are needed if the IRS ever examines your returns.  [[1]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/318-irs_publication_583_starting_a_business.pdf#page=16)  
- Records that are no longer needed for tax purposes should not be destroyed until you confirm whether you must keep them longer for other reasons (e.g., lender or insurance requirements).  [[1]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/318-irs_publication_583_starting_a_business.pdf#page=16)  

So, in general you keep tax records for the period of limitations applicable to that return, and employment‑tax records for at least four years.



**Sources:**
1. [irs_publication_583_starting_a_business.pdf (Page 16)](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/318-irs_publication_583_starting_a_business.pdf#page=16)

results.question: why do i need to keep business records
results.answer:
Business records are required for several practical and legal reasons:

1. **Recordkeeping is essential for monitoring and running a business.**  
   *“Everyone in business must keep records. Good records will help you do the following. Monitor the progress of your business. You need good records to monitor the progress of your business.” [[1]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/318-irs_publication_583_starting_a_business.pdf#page=11)*  

2. **They are needed to prepare accurate financial statements.**  
   *“Prepare your financial statements. You need good records to prepare accurate financial statements.” [[1]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/318-irs_publication_583_starting_a_business.pdf#page=11)*  

3. **Business records support tax reporting and compliance.**  
   *“It is important to keep these documents because they support the entries in your books and on your tax return.” [[2]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/318-irs_publication_583_starting_a_business.pdf#page=12)*  

4. **Records must be retained for the period the IRS may need them.**  
   *“You must keep your records as long as they may be needed for the administration of any provision of the Internal Revenue Code. Generally, this means you must keep records that support an item of income or deduction on a return until the period of limitations for that return runs out.” [[3]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/318-irs_publication_583_starting_a_business.pdf#page=16)*  

5. **Safety and regulatory compliance also require recordkeeping.**  
   *“Injury and illness records (OSHA 300, 300A, and 301) are kept at the worksite for at least five years.” [[4]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/319-osha_small_business_handbook.pdf#page=15)*  
   *“All work‑related fatalities are reported to OSHA within 8 hours.” [[4]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/319-osha_small_business_handbook.pdf#page=15)*  

By keeping proper records, you can monitor your business’s performance, prepare financial statements, satisfy tax and safety regulations, and provide the documentation the IRS and OSHA may request during inspections or audits.

results.question: what accounting method should i use
results.answer:
The IRS guidance says that the accounting method you pick depends mainly on whether your business holds inventory and on your size as a taxpayer.

**1. If you have no inventory**  
Most owners who do not keep inventory are advised to use the **cash method** because it is simpler: you record income when you receive it and expenses when you pay them – exactly the rule in the publications.

> *“Most individuals and many sole proprietors with no inventory use the cash method because they find it easier to keep cash‑method records.”* [[1]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/317-irs_publication_334_tax_guide_small_business.pdf#page=16)

**2. If you do hold inventory**  
When inventory is necessary to account for your income, the default is the **accrual method**. This is required unless you qualify as a small‑business taxpayer and can treat the inventory as non‑incidental material or supplies.

> *“If an inventory is necessary to account for your income, you must generally use an accrual method of accounting for sales and purchases unless you are a small business taxpayer (defined later in this chapter).”* [[1]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/317-irs_publication_334_tax_guide_small_business.pdf#page=16)

**3. Small‑business taxpayer definition**  
A small‑business taxpayer may use the cash method for inventory that is treated as non‑incidental materials or supplies:

> *“Small business taxpayer. You qualify as a small business taxpayer if you (a) have average annual gross receipts of $31 million or less for the 3 prior tax years (indexed for inflation), and (b) are not a tax shelter (as defined in section 448(d)(3)).”* [[1]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/317-irs_publication_334_tax_guide_small_business.pdf#page=16)

> *“Certain small business taxpayers can use the cash method of accounting and can also account for inventoriable items as materials and supplies that are not incidental.”* [[2]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/318-irs_publication_583_starting_a_business.pdf#page=5)

**Bottom line:**  

* Use the **cash method** if you **do not carry inventory**.  
* Use the **accrual method** if you carry inventory **and are not a qualifying small‑business taxpayer**.  
* If you **do** carry inventory **and qualify as a small‑business taxpayer**, you may treat the inventory as non‑incidental materials or supplies and still use the cash method.



**Sources:**

2. [irs_publication_583_starting_a_business.pdf (Page 5)](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/318-irs_publication_583_starting_a_business.pdf#page=5)

results.question: how do i check my workplace for hazards
results.answer:
**How to check your workplace for hazards**

1. **Conduct routine self‑inspections** – The handbook explains that “Workplace Self‑Inspection: An effective way to identify workplace hazards is for knowledgeable and experienced workers to conduct routine safety and health inspections (i.e. , self‑inspections). The only way to know if potential hazards exist and if they are under control is to assess work processes directly.” [[1]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/319-osha_small_business_handbook.pdf#page=8)

2. **Use the self‑inspection checklist** – The handbook contains a checklist that is “intended for general industry workplaces” and “can give you some indication where to begin taking action to make your business safer and more healthful for your workers.” [[1]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/319-osha_small_business_handbook.pdf#page=8)  
   *The checklist includes items such as:*
   * “A safety and health program is in place to help proactively manage safety and health in the workplace.”  
   * “Workers are trained how to identify and control hazards.”  
   * “Workplace inspections are conducted with workers.”  
   * …and many more. [[2]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/319-osha_small_business_handbook.pdf#page=9)

3. **Document the inspection** – The handbook provides a form:  
   *“Company name: Worksite: Specific worksite area: Inspected by: Date:” along with sections for general safety and health programs, hazard reporting, and control measures. [[2]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/319-osha_small_business_handbook.pdf#page=9)

4. **Compile data** – After completing the checklists, “Compile information from your completed checklists with workplace injury and illness records, worker training information, and process and equipment information (e.g. , maintenance logs, failure incident reports) to help you determine where challenges exist.” [[1]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/319-osha_small_business_handbook.pdf#page=8)

5. **Seek help if needed** – “Consultants from OSHA’s On‑Site Consultation programs … can help small business employers with this process at no cost.” [[1]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/319-osha_small_business_handbook.pdf#page=8)  

Follow these steps to identify, control, and monitor hazards in your workplace.

results.question: cash or accrual accounting whats the difference
results.answer:
**Cash‑method accounting**  
Under cash‑method accounting you record income only when you actually receive it and you normally deduct or capitalize expenses only in the year you actually pay them. The IRS explains it this way:  
> “Under the cash method, you report income in the tax year you receive it. You usually deduct or capitalize expenses in the tax year you pay them.” [[1]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/318-irs_publication_583_starting_a_business.pdf#page=5)

**Accrual‑method accounting**  
With the accrual method you report income in the year you earn it, even if payment is received later. Expenses are deducted or capitalized in the year they are incurred, regardless of when you pay them. The IRS explains it as:  
> “Under an accrual method, you generally report income in the tax year you earn it… You deduct or capitalize expenses in the tax year you incur them, whether or not you pay them that year.” [[1]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/318-irs_publication_583_starting_a_business.pdf#page=5)

**Key difference**  
The main distinction is the timing of when income and expenses are recognized:  
* Cash method → recognized when money actually changes hands.  
* Accrual method → recognized when the transaction is completed (right to receive income or obligation to pay expenses), not when payment is exchanged. [[2]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/317-irs_publication_334_tax_guide_small_business.pdf#page=15)



**Sources:**
1. [irs_publication_583_starting_a_business.pdf (Page 5)](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/318-irs_publication_583_starting_a_business.pdf#page=5)
2. [irs_publication_334_tax_guide_small_business.pdf (Page 15)](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/317-irs_publication_334_tax_guide_small_business.pdf#page=15)

results.question: can i deduct business travel
results.answer:
Yes.  The IRS allows a sole proprietor (or other business owner) to deduct ordinary and necessary expenses that arise when traveling away from your tax‑home for business.  The deduction is available for transportation, lodging, meals, and other travel‑related expenses, provided the trip meets the “away‑from‑home” test.  For example, the publication notes:

> “If you rent a car while away from home on business, you can deduct only the business‑use portion of the expenses…If you travel away from home, you can deduct the cost of travel by airplane, train, bus, or car between your home and your business destination.” [[1]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/317-irs_publication_334_tax_guide_small_business.pdf#page=40)

Meals and lodging are also deductible when the trip is overnight or long enough that you need to stop for sleep or rest to properly perform your duties.  You may deduct either actual expenses or the standard meal allowance, but in most cases only 50 % of meal expenses are deductible.  [[2]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/317-irs_publication_334_tax_guide_small_business.pdf#page=41)

The deduction can also include other travel‑related costs such as business telephone calls, parking, tolls, and dry‑cleaning while traveling.  [[2]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/317-irs_publication_334_tax_guide_small_business.pdf#page=41)

results.question: what goes in an executive summary
results.answer:
An executive summary is a very short, stand‑alone section that gives the reader a quick look at the core of your business plan.  According to the SBA Business Planning Guide it should

* be only one or two paragraphs,  
* give an overview of what you want to accomplish, and  
* include the key facts that will matter most to a reader such as:  
  * your business idea,  
  * how much money you need and what it will be used for,  
  * how much money you will bring (or have already invested) into the business, and  
  * a brief schedule of your goals.  

Because many of these details are best known after the rest of the plan is written, the guide recommends writing the executive summary last.

results.question: do i have to make my shop wheelchair accessible
results.answer:
Yes.  Your shop is a private business that serves the public, so it is a **public accommodation** under the ADA.  The agency requires that any **barrier that is “readily achievable” be removed** (or an alternative be provided).

* “Private businesses that provide goods or services to the public are called public accommodations in the ADA … If you own, operate, lease, or lease‑to a business that serves the public, then you are covered by the ADA and have obligations for existing facilities …” [[1]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/316-ada_guide_small_business.pdf#page=6)

* “If you own or operate a business that serves the public you must remove physical “barriers” that are “readily achievable,” which means …” [[2]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/316-ada_guide_small_business.pdf#page=12)

* “When a business has two public entrances, in most cases, only one must be accessible … If one entrance is not accessible and another entrance is accessible, a sign must provide direction to the accessible entrance … When a ramp is added to provide an accessible entrance, the slope of the ramp should be … not more than 1:12 … handrails … (if the slope is more than 1:20) …” [[3]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/316-ada_guide_small_business.pdf#page=10)

In practice, this means you must:

1. **Provide at least one entrance that is accessible**—or, if you cannot modify the existing entrance, add a ramp or an alternative entrance that meets the ramp and door width requirements;  
2. **Make the door width at least 36 inches** (or widen older doors that are 32 inches) and install accessible hardware (lever handle, loop‑type pull, etc.) [[2]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/316-ada_guide_small_business.pdf#page=12);  
3. **Meet the 1:12 ramp slope and handrail requirements** if you install a ramp [[3]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/316-ada_guide_small_business.pdf#page=10).

If any of these changes are not “readily achievable” due to your resources or the structure of your shop, you may delay them, but you must plan to remove the barrier when it becomes feasible.  

So, in short, you *must* make your shop wheelchair‑accessible in any way that is readily achievable.

results.question: am i exempt from injury recordkeeping
results.answer:
You are exempt from the OSHA injury‑ and illness‑recordkeeping requirements only if **both** of the following conditions are met:

1. **You had 10 or fewer employees during every calendar year,** or  
2. **Your business is in one of the specific low‑hazard industries listed in 29 CFR 1904, Subpart B, Appendix A.**

All other employers, no matter their size or industry, must still keep OSHA Forms 300, 301, and 300A and must report fatalities, in‑patient hospitalizations, amputations, and loss of an eye to OSHA.  

> “NOTE: Employers are partially exempt from OSHA’s injury and illness recordkeeping requirements if 1) they had 10 or fewer workers during all of the last calendar year (see 29 CFR 1904.1), or 2) they are in certain low‑hazard industries (see 29 CFR Part 1904, Subpart B, Appendix A). All employers, regardless of size or industry, must report work-related fatalities, in-patient hospitalizations, amputations, and loss of an eye to OSHA.”  
> [[1]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/319-osha_small_business_handbook.pdf#page=14)

**How to start a business and keep your taxes organized**

1. **Choose the type of business and register it**  
   • Decide whether it will be a sole‑prop, partnership, corporation, or LLC.  The document explains the decision point:  
     *"Determining Which Type of Business to Use – The most common forms of business are the sole proprietorship, partnership, and corporation."* [[1]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/318-irs_publication_583_starting_a_business.pdf#page=2)  
   • Register the business name.  If you use a fictitious name, you must file a statement:  
     *"You are required to file a fictitious name statement if you operate a business as a proprietorship or partnership and do not include the last name of each owner in the business name."* [[2]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/320-sba_business_planning_guide.pdf#page=6)  
   • Obtain a federal Employer Identification Number (EIN) if you have employees or if you choose to operate under a name other than your SSN:  
     *"If your business will hire employees or pay Federal Excise Tax, a Federal Employer's Identification Number (EIN) must be obtained from Internal Revenue Service."* [[2]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/320-sba_business_planning_guide.pdf#page=6)

2. **Decide on a tax year and accounting method**  
   • Pick a calendar tax year (January 1 – December 31) or a fiscal tax year.  The choice must be reported and often must be approved by the IRS:  
     *"If you adopt the calendar‑tax year, you must maintain your books and records and report your income and expenses for the period from January 1 through December 31 of each year."* [[3]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/317-irs_publication_334_tax_guide_small_business.pdf#page=14)  
   • Select an accounting method that clearly shows your income (cash, accrual, or a hybrid).  The method must be used consistently and is used when you file your first tax return:  
     *"You choose an accounting method for your business when you file your first income tax return that includes a Schedule C (Form 1040) for the business."* [[3]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/317-irs_publication_334_tax_guide_small_business.pdf#page=14)

3. **Keep a record‑keeping system**  
   • Set up books that summarize all business transactions.  These can be simple journals and a ledger, or a more sophisticated program, but they should always show gross income, deductions, and credits:  
     *"Your recordkeeping system should include a summary of your business transactions. This summary is ordinarily made in your books (for example, accounting journals and ledgers)."* [[4]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/318-irs_publication_583_starting_a_business.pdf#page=12)  
   • Store supporting documents (sales slips, invoices, receipts, deposit slips, canceled checks, bank statements, etc.) to back every book entry:  
     *"Supporting Documents…include sales slips, paid bills, invoices, receipts, deposit slips, and canceled checks."* [[5]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/318-irs_publication_583_starting_a_business.pdf#page=13)  
   • If you use an electronic system, keep it indexed, preserve, retrieve, and reproduce it in a legible format for the IRS:  
     *"The electronic storage system must index, store, preserve, retrieve, and reproduce the electronically stored books and records in legible format."* [[4]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/318-irs_publication_583_starting_a_business.pdf#page=12)

4. **Maintain specific records for tax purposes**  
   • **Gross receipts** – keep bank deposit slips, cash register tapes, and receipt books:  
     *"Goods receipts. Gross receipts are the income you receive from your business... Documents that show gross receipts include the following: • Cash register tapes. • Bank deposit slips. • Receipt books."* [[5]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/318-irs_publication_583_starting_a_business.pdf#page=13)  
   • **Business expenses** – record every expense, noting date, amount, and purpose; keep receipts or invoices; and separate personal vs. business use:  
     *"Keep supporting documents that show the amounts and sources of your gross receipts... Keep them in an orderly fashion and in a safe place."* [[4]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/318-irs_publication_583_starting_a_business.pdf#page=12)  
   • **Employment records** – if you have employees, keep at least 4 years of records:  
     *"Employment taxes. If you have employees, you must keep all employment tax records for at least 4 years after the date the tax becomes due or is paid, whichever is later."* [[6]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/318-irs_publication_583_starting_a_business.pdf#page=16)  
   • **Asset documents** – keep purchase and sale invoices, closing statements, and anything that shows cost and use for depreciation purposes:  
     *"Your records should show the following information… Purchase price. Cost of any improvements. Section 179 deduction taken. Deductions taken for depreciation."* [[5]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/318-irs_publication_583_starting_a_business.pdf#page=13)

5. **Know how long to keep records**  
   • Keep records for the period of limitations for the return (usually 3–4 years) or longer if required by other agencies:  
     *"You must keep your records as long as they may be needed for the administration of any provision of the Internal Revenue Code… Generally, this means you must keep records that support an item of income or deduction on a return until the period of limitations for that return runs out."* [[6]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/318-irs_publication_583_starting_a_business.pdf#page=16)

6. **File the correct forms and report on time**  
   • If you are a single‑owner, file Form 1040 with Schedule C.  Attach a separate Schedule C for each business if you own more than one:  
     *"If you operated more than one business as a sole proprietorship, attach a separate Schedule C (Form 1040) for each business."* [[7]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/317-irs_publication_334_tax_guide_small_business.pdf#page=7)  
   • Use the IRS e‑file option if available; it speeds processing and reduces errors:

results.answer:
To keep your employees safe and your premises accessible, the documents provide the following concrete requirements and actions:

---

### 1. Protect your employees from workplace hazards  
**Walk‑Working Surfaces (OSHA Small‑Business Handbook)**  

- Keep all walking‑working surfaces clean, orderly, and sanitary.  
  *[cite this passage as: [[1]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/319-osha_small_business_handbook.pdf#page=78)]*  
- Cover or repair holes, slatted floors, and other obstructions; use guardrails or covers that can withstand twice the maximum intended load.  
  *[cite this passage as: [[1]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/319-osha_small_business_handbook.pdf#page=78)]*  
- Supply wet surfaces with non‑slip materials, maintain drainage, and use false floors or mats where feasible.  
  *[cite this passage as: [[1]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/319-osha_small_business_handbook.pdf#page=78)]*  
- Arrange aisles and walkways so workers are not exposed to moving machinery, welding operations, or other hazards.  
  *[cite this passage as: [[1]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/319-osha_small_business_handbook.pdf#page=78)]*  
- Ensure clear headroom, provide adequate guardrails for elevated surfaces more than 4 ft (1.2 m), and use fall protection where required.  
  *[cite this passage as: [[1]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/319-osha_small_business_handbook.pdf#page=78)]*  
  *[cite this passage as: [[2]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/319-osha_small_business_handbook.pdf#page=73)]*  
- Conduct routine inspections and promptly repair or remove any identified hazards.  
  *[cite this passage as: [[1]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/319-osha_small_business_handbook.pdf#page=78)]*

**Key takeaway** – The handbook’s “Walkways” checklist is the starting point for all safety inspections; complete it regularly and act on any problem that the checklist flags.

---

### 2. Keep pedestrian access safe and easily navigable  
**Accessible Entrance (ADA Guide for Small Business)**  

- If you add a ramp, its slope must be as gentle as possible but never steeper than **1:12**.  
  *[cite this passage as: [[3]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/316-ada_guide_small_business.pdf#page=10)]*  
- If the ramp’s slope is steeper than **1:20** and the vertical rise exceeds 6 inches, install handrails (and edge protection).  
  *[cite this passage as: [[3]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/316-ada_guide_small_business.pdf#page=10)]*  
- Provide edge protection (e.g., a lower railing) where a drop‑off occurs to prevent people from rolling off a ramp.  
  *[cite this passage as: [[4]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/316-ada_guide_small_business.pdf#page=11)]*  
- When an alternate entrance is not available, make an accessible way to the store (home delivery, curbside service, etc.) **if readily achievable**.  
  *[cite this passage as: [[4]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/316-ada_guide_small_business.pdf#page=11)]*  

**Key takeaway** – A compliant entrance needs a ramp with the correct slope, handrails when required, and no steps or sharp drop‑offs.

---

### 3. Maintain door and hardware that allows people with disabilities to enter  
**Door Hardware (ADA Guide for Small Business)**  

- Doors should open to at least **36 inches** clear width (or 32 inches if older).  
  *[cite this passage as: [[5]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/316-ada_guide_small_business.pdf#page=12)]*  
- Replace any lever‑type, plate‑type, or thumb‑latch hardware that requires tight grasping, twisting, or pinching with a lever handle, loop handle, or other accessible option.  
  *[cite this passage as: [[5]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/316-ada_guide_small_business.pdf#page=12)]*  
- For narrow revolving turnstiles, provide an accessible gate or opening **if doing so is readily achievable**.  
  *[cite this passage as: [[5]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/316-ada_guide_small_business.pdf#page=12)]*  

**Key takeaway** – A single accessible door and hardware upgrade can solve many access problems.

---

### 4. Offer accessible parking and routes to the building  
**Accessible Parking (ADA Guide for Small Business)**  

- Designate at least one accessible parking space per **≤ 25** spaces and a second for **≤ 50** spaces; at least one of these must be a **van‑accessible** space.  
  *[cite this passage as: [[6]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/316-ada_guide_small_business.pdf#page=9)]*  
- Each accessible space requires an access aisle that is five‑feet wide for cars (eight feet for vans).  
  *[cite this passage as: [[7]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/316-ada_guide_small_business.pdf#page=8)]*  
- Provide a **98‑inch vertical clearance** on the vehicular route, at the space, and to an exit.  
  *[cite this passage as: [[7]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/316-ada_guide_small_business.pdf#page=8)]*  
- Mount the international symbol of accessibility on the space (and “van‑accessible” for van spaces) high enough to avoid being hidden by a parked car.  
  *[cite this passage as: [[7]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/316-ada_guide_small_business.pdf#page=8)]*  

**Key takeaway** – Accessible parking must be located close to an accessible entrance and on a level, smooth route.

results.question: how do i write a business plan and set up accounting
results.answer:
**Writing a Business Plan (SBA Business Planning Guide)**  

1. **Start with the outline** – The guide gives a suggested structure: Cover Page, Executive Summary, Business, Management, Market, Money, and Exhibits.  
   *It says: “The following is a suggested outline of the material that should be included in your business plan” [[1]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/320-sba_business_planning_guide.pdf#page=4).*

2. **Cover Page** – Include company name, address, phone, owners, and date.  
   *“The cover page is the first impression of your business plan… include the name of the company, company address, company phone number, owners and their addresses/phone numbers, and the date of the plan” [[1]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/320-sba_business_planning_guide.pdf#page=4).*

3. **Executive Summary** – One‑two paragraphs summarizing idea, capital needed, and schedule.  
   *“This portion should be brief; usually one or two paragraphs, but it should give the reader an overview of your business” [[1]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/320-sba_business_planning_guide.pdf#page=4).*

4. **Business Section** – Describe industry, product/service, competitive advantage, regulations, facilities, and equipment.  
   *“Describe your product(s)… outline your product or service in terms of marketability” [[2]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/320-sba_business_planning_guide.pdf#page=12).  “Describe any regulations that affect the sale and use of your product” [[2]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/320-sba_business_planning_guide.pdf#page=12).*

5. **Management Section** – Detail business organization, owners’ ownership percentages, key personnel, and accounting responsibilities.  
   *“Identify who has primary operational, marketing and accounting responsibilities and their qualifications to do so” [[3]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/320-sba_business_planning_guide.pdf#page=13).*

6. **Market Section** – Provide total and target market size, competition, and promotion plan.  
   *“The marketing plan includes information on the total market… competition and how you plan to make and promote your product/service available” [[1]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/320-sba_business_planning_guide.pdf#page=4).*

7. **Money Section** – Include:
   * **Historical financial statements** (if any)
   * **Three‑year income projection**
   * **Cash‑flow projection**
   * **Break‑even analysis**
   * **Sources and uses of funds**  
   *“Documents that should be included… summary of financial need, 3‑year income projection, statement of cash flow, balance sheet, break‑even analysis” [[4]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/320-sba_business_planning_guide.pdf#page=16).*

8. **Exhibits** – Attach resumes, contracts, floor plans, credit reports, lease agreements, and any other supporting documents.  
   *“Include documents needed to substantiate what you have presented… examples would include resumes, purchase agreements, bids, contracts, floor plans, etc.” [[1]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/320-sba_business_planning_guide.pdf#page=4).*

9. **Use the “checklist”** – The SBA guide also lists practical items to verify during planning, such as confirming legal entity, licensing, and feasibility data.  
   *“Consult your counselor if you have any questions on what to include” [[1]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/320-sba_business_planning_guide.pdf#page=4).*

---

**Setting Up Accounting (IRS Publication 583 & 334)**  

1. **Choose an accounting method** – Cash or accrual.  
   *“Choosing an accounting method… The most common methods are any of the following: Cash method, an accrual method, special methods, or a combination” [[5]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/317-irs_publication_334_tax_guide_small_business.pdf#page=14).*  
   *“You choose an accounting method for your business when you file your first income tax return” [[6]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/318-irs_publication_583_starting_a_business.pdf#page=5).*

2. **Determine whether you need inventory accounting** – If you sell, produce, or purchase merchandise, inventory is required and an accrual method is typically needed.  
   *“If you produce, purchase, or sell merchandise… you must keep an inventory and use an accrual method” [[7]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/317-irs_publication_334_tax_guide_small_business.pdf#page=17).*

3. **Set up a bookkeeping system** –  
   * **Single‑entry** – simplest, tracks cash receipts and disbursements.  
   * **Double‑entry** – uses journals and ledgers, balances debits and credits.  
   *“A single‑entry system is based on the income statement… A double‑entry bookkeeping system uses journals and ledgers” [[8]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/318-irs_publication_583_starting_a_business.pdf#page=15).*

4. **Create a chart of accounts** – Lists all income, expense, asset, liability, and equity accounts.  
   *The guide notes the importance of a detailed chart of accounts but does not give a page number for a specific definition, so this is inferred from the accounting section.*  

5. **Record transactions** –  
   * **Journal entry example:** rent expense debit, cash credit (shown on page 15 of the IRS guide).  
   *“Each account has a left side for debits and a right side for credits… the total debits must equal the total credits” [[8]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/318-irs_publication_583_starting_a_business.pdf#page=15).*

6. **Close books at year‑end** – Close income and expense accounts to retained earnings or capital accounts.  
   *“You close income and expense accounts at the end of each tax year” [[8]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/318-irs_publication_583_starting_a_business.pdf#page=15).*

7. **Keep detailed records** – Machine‑sensible records must match your books and be able to support returns.  
   *“You must be able to produce sufficient legible records to support and verify entries” [[8]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/318-irs_publication_583_starting_a_business.pdf#page=15).*

8. **File required tax returns** – All businesses file the proper forms (e.g., Schedule C for sole proprietors).

results.question: what should i track for taxes and for travel expenses
results.answer:
**What to track for taxes**

1. **Income and receipts** – Keep every source of money you receive: cash register tapes, bank deposit slips, receipt books, invoices, and electronic statements.  *[[1]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/318-irs_publication_583_starting_a_business.pdf#page=11)*  

2. **Deductible business expenses** – Record every expense that is ordinary and necessary for your trade or business (e.g., supplies, utilities, office rent, travel).  *[[1]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/318-irs_publication_583_starting_a_business.pdf#page=11)*  

3. **Supporting documents** – For every expense, keep a receipt, invoice, canceled check, or other proof of payment.  *[[2]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/318-irs_publication_583_starting_a_business.pdf#page=12)*  

4. **Tax‑specific records** –  
   * **Employment taxes** – Keep payroll records, payroll tax filings, and related notices for at least 4 years.  *[[3]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/318-irs_publication_583_starting_a_business.pdf#page=16)*  
   * **Excise taxes** – Maintain records of any excise taxes paid and the forms you file (e.g., Form 720, 2290).  *[[4]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/318-irs_publication_583_starting_a_business.pdf#page=8)*  
   * **Information returns** – Preserve copies of 1099‑MISC, 1099‑NEC, W‑2, and Form 8300 where applicable.  *[[4]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/318-irs_publication_583_starting_a_business.pdf#page=8)*  

5. **Retention period** – Keep all these records for the period of limitations that applies to the tax year; generally until the limit period for that return runs out (usually 3 years for income tax, longer for other taxes).  *[[3]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/318-irs_publication_583_starting_a_business.pdf#page=16)*  

---

**What to track for travel expenses**

Track the same basic items (date, amount, purpose, payee) for each travel‑related transaction, and also the specific categories that the IRS allows to be deducted:

| Category | What to record | Example |
|----------|---------------|---------|
| **Transportation** – airfare, train, bus, car rental, taxi, commuter bus, limousine | Date, carrier, class (business/first class), fare, mileage | Flight Blue Air NYC‑LAX, $350 |
| **Taxi, commuter bus, limousine** – fares between airport/​station and hotel or work location | Amount, date, destination | Taxi from LAX to Hotel, $45 |
| **Baggage and shipping** – cost of sending baggage or samples | Weight, destination, receipt | $12 for sample shipment to client |
| **Car or truck (actual or mileage)** – maintenance, fuel, tolls, parking (only business‑related parts) | Miles driven, fuel cost, repair receipts | 200 miles, $30 fuel, tolls $10 |
| **Meals and lodging** – costs of meals and overnight lodging | Date, location, business purpose, amounts | Hotel $150/night, meal $45 |
| **Cleaning, laundry** – costs for maintaining travel gear | Amount, date | Dry‑cleaning $20 |
| **Telephone** – business calls made while traveling | Date, number called, purpose | $15 for conference call |
| **Tips** – to hotel staff, drivers, etc. | Amount | $10 tip to taxi driver |

The IRS notes that you may deduct **50 %** of meal expenses (unless the meal is provided by a motel or other lodging where the expense is included).  *[[5]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/317-irs_publication_334_tax_guide_small_business.pdf#page=41)*  

Travel expenses are deductible when the trip is **away from home** for business, meeting both the “away from home” and “rest/sleep” conditions.  *[[6]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/317-irs_publication_334_tax_guide_small_business.pdf#page=40)*  

**Record‑keeping for travel**

* Keep a travel log or mileage log that records date, origin, destination, purpose, and miles traveled.  
* Save receipts for all transportation, lodging, meals, shipping, parking, tolls, and other travel costs.  
* For mileage, note business mileage separately from personal mileage so you can apportion actual expenses or calculate the standard mileage rate.  *[[1]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/318-irs_publication_583_starting_a_business.pdf#page=11)*  

By tracking these items accurately and keeping the supporting documents for the required retention period, you’ll have the records needed to satisfy both tax reporting and deductible travel‑expense claims.

results.question: do i need an ein and what accounting method comes with it
results.answer:
Yes.  
The IRS requires a Taxpayer Identification Number (TIN) for all businesses that must file tax returns, pay wages, or file pension or excise‑tax returns.  The most common TINs are a Social‑Security number (SSN) for individuals and an Employer Identification Number (EIN) for any other business entity (including sole‑proprietors).  The documents state:

- “EINs are assigned to *sole proprietors, LLCs, corporations, and partnerships* for tax filing and reporting purposes.” [[1]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/318-irs_publication_583_starting_a_business.pdf#page=4)  
- “You must also have an EIN to use as a TIN if you do either of the following: *Pay wages to one or more employees* or *File pension or excise tax returns*.” [[2]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/317-irs_publication_334_tax_guide_small_business.pdf#page=6)  

**Accounting method**

When you file your first income‑tax return you must also choose an accounting method.  The only methods you can choose from at that time are:

- **Cash method** – income is reported when received and expenses when paid.  
- **Accrual method** – income is reported when earned (even if payment comes later) and expenses when incurred.  

The publications describe the choice:

- “You choose an accounting method for your business **when you file your first income tax return**.” [[3]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/318-irs_publication_583_starting_a_business.pdf#page=5)  
- “There are two basic accounting methods: **1. Cash method** … **2. Accrual method**.” [[3]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/318-irs_publication_583_starting_a_business.pdf#page=5)  

So, if you are forming a business that will pay employees, file special tax returns, or simply want a separate TIN, you need an EIN.  When you file your first tax return, you will select either the cash method or the accrual method (depending on whether you have inventory or other factors).

runs.question: how long do i keep tax records
runs.answer:
When the IRS tells you to keep a record, it is for a specific period that depends on the type of record.  Below is the retention schedule that appears in the IRS publication on record‑keeping for small businesses:

* **All tax‑related records that support income or deductions** – keep them **“as long as they may be needed for the administration of any provision of the Internal Revenue Code.”**  This means you keep them until the period of limitations for that return expires.  The period of limitations is the time during which you can amend a return to claim a credit or refund, or the IRS can assess additional tax.  [[1]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/318-irs_publication_583_starting_a_business.pdf#page=16)

* **Employment‑tax records** – keep them **at least 4 years after the date the tax becomes due or is paid, whichever is later.**  [[1]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/318-irs_publication_583_starting_a_business.pdf#page=16)

* **Asset records** – keep records that relate to property **until the period of limitations expires for the year in which you dispose of the property** in a taxable disposition.  These records are needed to calculate depreciation, amortization, depletion, and the basis of the property.  [[1]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/318-irs_publication_583_starting_a_business.pdf#page=16)

* **Records no longer needed for tax purposes** – do not discard them until you find out whether you have to keep them longer for another reason (e.g., insurance, creditors).  [[1]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/318-irs_publication_583_starting_a_business.pdf#page=16)

These guidelines cover the required retention periods for the kinds of documents that most small businesses generate. If you have specific situations (e.g., an audit or an appeal), you may need to keep records longer, but the above are the minimum periods dictated by IRS policy.

runs.question: what accounting method should i use
runs.answer:
The IRS documents explain which method you should use in two main situations.

**1. Cash method – usually the default for most small‑business owners**

> “Most individuals and many sole proprietors with no inventory use the cash method because they find it easier to keep cash‑method records.”  
>  [[1]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/317-irs_publication_334_tax_guide_small_business.pdf#page=14)

If you ​do​ not keep inventory, the cash method is appropriate.  
Other IRS guidance confirms this.  
> “If an inventory is necessary to account for your income, you must generally use an accrual method of accounting … unless you are a small business taxpayer.”  
>  [[2]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/318-irs_publication_583_starting_a_business.pdf#page=5)

**2. Accrual method – required when inventory is needed (unless you qualify as a small‑business taxpayer)**  

> “If an inventory is necessary to account for your income, you must generally use an accrual method of accounting for purchases and sales.”  
>  [[1]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/317-irs_publication_334_tax_guide_small_business.pdf#page=14)

Even if you do have inventory, the accrual method is compulsory unless you meet the “small‑business‑taxpayer” criteria:

> “Small business taxpayer. You qualify as a small business taxpayer if you (a) have average annual gross receipts of $31 million or less for the 3 prior tax years, and (b) are not a tax shelter.”  
>  [[3]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/317-irs_publication_334_tax_guide_small_business.pdf#page=16)

If you qualify, you can still use the cash method **provided** your inventory is treated as non‑incidental materials or supplies (i.e., items that are not inventory in the traditional sense).  

> “Certain small business taxpayers can use the cash method… and can also account for inventoriable items as materials and supplies that are not incidental.”  
>  [[2]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/318-irs_publication_583_starting_a_business.pdf#page=5)

**In practice**

- **Use the cash method** if you are a sole proprietor or small business with **no inventory** or if your inventory qualifies as non‑incidental materials and you meet the small‑business gross‑receipt test.  
- **Use the accrual method** if you keep inventory that is *inventoriable* (goods sold or used in production) and you do **not** meet the small‑business gross‑receipt threshold, or you simply prefer a method that matches income with the time it is earned.

These decisions must be made when you file your first business tax return that includes a Schedule C (Form 1040).  Changing the method later generally requires IRS approval.  [[1]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/317-irs_publication_334_tax_guide_small_business.pdf#page=14)

runs.question: cash or accrual accounting whats the difference
runs.answer:
Cash‑method accounting and accrual‑method accounting differ primarily in **when** income and expenses are recorded for tax purposes.

**Cash method**  
- Income is reported in the tax year it is **received**.  
- Expenses are generally deducted in the tax year they are **paid**.  
- Example: if you receive a $500 payment on December 30 2025 that you can’t deposit until January 3 2026, you must include the payment in 2025 income but can deduct the expense in 2025 only if it is paid in 2025 (IRS Pub. 583, page 5).  
- The method is simple and is often used by owners who have little or no inventory (IRS Pub. 583, page 5).

**Accrual method**  
- Income is reported in the tax year it is **earned**—when you are entitled to it, even if you receive payment later.  
- Expenses are deducted or capitalized in the tax year they are **incurred**—when the obligation is established, even if payment is made later.  
- Example: if you deliver a product on December 28 2025 but are not paid until February 2026, you must include the revenue in 2025 and you can deduct the expense in 2025 if the liability has been established and its amount is reasonably determinable (IRS Pub. 334, page 15‑16).  
- The accrual method matches income and related expenses in the same year, which is why it is required whenever inventory is used (IRS Pub. 583, page 5).

Key points that separate the two methods  

| Feature | Cash Method | Accrual Method |
|---------|-------------|----------------|
| **Income timing** | When received | When earned |
| **Expense timing** | When paid | When incurred |
| **Inventory rule** | Can be used with or without inventory (small‑business exception) | Required if inventory is needed (IRS Pub. 583, page 5) |
| **Matching principle** | Not required | Required – income matched with related expenses |

These distinctions are the core of the difference between cash and accrual accounting as defined by the IRS.

runs.question: can i deduct business travel
runs.answer:
Yes.  If you travel away from home for work, the IRS allows you to deduct the ordinary and necessary expenses of that trip—including transportation, lodging, and meals (at 50 % of the cost).  The deduction applies to trips that are overnight or require you to sleep or rest to perform your duties.  For example, the publication states:

> “Meals and lodging. You can deduct the cost of meals and lodging if your business trip is overnight or long enough that you need to stop for sleep or rest to properly perform your duties. You can use actual expenses or the standard meal allowance to calculate your deduction. In most cases, you can deduct only 50% of your meal expenses.” [[1]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/317-irs_publication_334_tax_guide_small_business.pdf#page=41)

> “Travel expenses. These are the ordinary and necessary expenses of traveling away from home for your business… You are traveling away from home if both the following conditions are met… 1. Your duties require you to be away from the general area of your tax home substantially longer than an ordinary day’s work. 2. You need to get sleep or rest to meet the demands of your work while away from home.” [[2]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/317-irs_publication_334_tax_guide_small_business.pdf#page=40)

However, commuting between your home and your regular or main place of business is **not** deductible.  The rule is:

> “You can’t deduct the costs of driving your car or truck between your home and your main or regular workplace. These costs are personal commuting expenses.” [[3]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/317-irs_publication_334_tax_guide_small_business.pdf#page=35)

So you can deduct travel expenses for business trips that meet the “away‑from‑home” criteria, but you cannot deduct normal commuting costs.

runs.question: what goes in an executive summary
runs.answer:
An executive summary is a brief overview—usually one to two paragraphs—of the business plan. It should give the reader a quick snapshot of what you want to accomplish, covering:

* your business idea,
* how much money you need and what you will use it for,
* how much money you have already invested (or plan to bring in),
* and a short schedule of your key goals.

Because some of these details are only clear after the rest of the plan is finished, the executive summary is written last.

runs.question: how do i describe my target market
runs.answer:
To clearly describe your target market in a business plan, follow the structure suggested in the SBA Business Planning Guide:

1. **Identify the niche and best customer**  
   Describe who your most valuable customers are and why they are your focus.  
   _“Describe your market niche; who is your best customer. Identify those customers and describe their characteristics.” [[1]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/320-sba_business_planning_guide.pdf#page=14)_

2. **Segment the market (business or consumer)**  
   *Business markets*: segment by industry, company size, location, or product use/application.  
   *Consumer markets*: segment by demographics (age, gender), geographic location, economic status, lifestyle, product application, or benefits sought.  
   _“Business markets might be classified by industry, company size, location, or product use/application. Consumer (household) markets might be segmented by demographics, (age, gender), geographic location, economic status, lifestyle, product application or benefits sought.” [[1]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/320-sba_business_planning_guide.pdf#page=14)_

3. **Estimate size and growth potential**  
   Use population figures, sales tax data, industry reports or other credible sources to estimate the total market size and how much of it you expect to capture.  
   _“Estimate the approximate size and growth potential of the target market(s) using population figures, sales tax info, industry information, etc. Estimate how much of the total market you will capture.” [[2]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/320-sba_business_planning_guide.pdf#page=15)_

4. **Present the information concisely**  
   A succinct paragraph or table summarizing the niche, key characteristics, segmentation criteria, market size, and growth projection is usually sufficient and keeps the reader focused on the most important facts.  

These steps provide a clear, evidence‑based description of the target market that satisfies the requirements of a standard business plan.

runs.question: do i have to make my shop wheelchair accessible
runs.answer:
Yes.  The ADA Guide for Small Businesses states that a shop that is open to the public must give people who use wheelchairs or other mobility devices a way to enter and use the place.  
- “Providing physical access to a facility from public sidewalks, public transportation, or parking is basic to making goods and services available to people with disabilities.” [[1]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/316-ada_guide_small_business.pdf#page=10)  
- “If a business has two public entrances, in most cases, only one must be accessible.” [[1]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/316-ada_guide_small_business.pdf#page=10)  

When you have an accessible entrance, the rest of the shop must also be usable:  

- “When sales or service counters are provided, the counters must be accessible, if doing so is readily achievable.” [[2]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/316-ada_guide_small_business.pdf#page=15)  
- “If you cannot provide an accessible sales or service counter or auxiliary counter nearby…you may provide a clipboard or lap board for use until a more permanent solution can be implemented.” [[2]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/316-ada_guide_small_business.pdf#page=15)

So, unless it is not *readily achievable* for some part of the shop, you need to make at least one entrance, and the sales area and counters, wheelchair‑accessible.

runs.question: am i exempt from injury recordkeeping
runs.answer:
You are exempt from the OSHA injury‑and‑illness recordkeeping requirements only if you meet one of the following conditions (as stated in *osha_small_business_handbook.pdf*):

- You had **10 or fewer workers during all of the last calendar year**, or  
- You are in a **low‑hazard industry** (see 29 CFR Part 1904, Subpart B, Appendix A).

> [cite this passage as: [[1]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/319-osha_small_business_handbook.pdf#page=14)]

All employers, regardless of size or industry, must still report **work‑related fatalities, in‑patient hospitalizations, amputations, and loss of an eye** to OSHA.

runs.question: what records do i keep for tax and for injuries and for how long
runs.answer:
**What records do you need to keep for tax purposes, and how long must you keep them?**  
(See IRS *Publication 583 – Starting a Business* (2024).)  

- **All records that support an item of income or deduction on a tax return** must be kept **as long as they may be needed for the administration of any provision of the Internal Revenue Code**.  
  - “You must keep your records as long as they may be needed for the administration of any provision of the Internal Revenue Code. Generally, this means you must keep records that support an item of income or deduction on a return until the period of limitations for that return runs out.” [[1]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/318-irs_publication_583_starting_a_business.pdf#page=16)  

- **Employment‑tax records** (e.g., W‑2s, payroll records, Forms 941, 944, 940) must be kept **for at least 4 years after the date the tax becomes due or is paid, whichever is later**.  
  - “Employment taxes. If you have employees, you must keep all employment tax records for at least 4 years after the date the tax becomes due or is paid, whichever is later.” [[1]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/318-irs_publication_583_starting_a_business.pdf#page=16)  

- **Copies of filed tax returns** should be retained for future reference, and keep them “until the period of limitations…expires.”  
  - “Keep copies of your filed tax returns. They help in preparing future tax returns and making calculations if you file an amended return.” [[1]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/318-irs_publication_583_starting_a_business.pdf#page=16)  

- **Asset‑related records** (depreciation, cost basis, disposal statements) must be kept until the period of limitations expires for the year in which the property is disposed of in a taxable disposition.  
  - “Keep records relating to property until the period of limitations expires for the year in which you dispose of the property in a taxable disposition.” [[1]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/318-irs_publication_583_starting_a_business.pdf#page=16)  

---

**What records do you need to keep for injuries/illnesses, and how long must you keep them?**  
(See *OSHA Small Business Safety and Health Handbook*.)  

- **Injury and illness records** (OSHA Form 300 Log, OSHA Form 301 Incident Report, and the annual summary Form 300A) must be kept **for at least five (5) years**.  
  - “Injury and illness records (OSHA 300, 300A, and 301) are kept at the worksite for at least five years.” [[2]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/319-osha_small_business_handbook.pdf#page=15)  

- **Worker medical and exposure records** must be retained “for the time period required for each specific type of record.”  
  - “Worker medical and exposure records are retained for the time period required for each specific type of record.” [[2]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/319-osha_small_business_handbook.pdf#page=15)  

- **Worker training records** must be kept and accessible for review by workers as required by OSHA standards.  
  - “Worker training records are kept and accessible for review by workers, as required by OSHA standards.” [[2]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/319-osha_small_business_handbook.pdf#page=15)  

- **Fatalities** (and in‑patient hospitalizations, amputations, and loss of an eye) must be reported **to OSHA within 8 hours**; more severe cases (hospitalizations, amputations, loss of an eye) within **24 hours**.  
  - “All work‑related fatalities are reported to OSHA within 8 hours. All work‑related in‑patient hospitalizations, amputations, and loss of an eye are reported to OSHA within 24 hours.” [[2]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/319-osha_small_business_handbook.pdf#page=15)  

- **Electronic submission of annual summary** (Form 300A) is required **by March 2 of the year after the calendar year covered** if you meet the size and industry thresholds described in the handbook.  
  - “You must electronically submit information from your Form 300A Summary to OSHA annually (by March 2 of the year after the calendar year covered by the form)” [[2]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/319-osha_small_business_handbook.pdf#page=15)  

---

**Bottom line:**  
- **Tax records:** keep until the IRS period of limitations expires; keep employment‑tax records for 4 years (or longer if needed for other purposes); keep asset records until the related tax year’s limitations expires.  
- **Injury/illness records:** keep OSHA forms 300, 300A, 301 and all related medical, exposure, and training records for at least 5 years (or the required period for specific medical records).  

These retention periods are mandated by the IRS and OSHA documents cited above.



**Sources:**
1. [irs_publication_583_starting_a_business.pdf (Page 16)](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/318-irs_publication_583_starting_a_business.pdf#page=16)
2. [osha_small_business_handbook.pdf (Page 15)](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/319-osha_small_business_handbook.pdf#page=15)

runs.question: what do i need to do to keep employees safe and my premises accessible
runs.answer:
**Keep your employees safe**

1. **Implement a safety and health program** that follows OSHA’s seven core elements: management leadership, worker participation, hazard identification & assessment, hazard prevention & control, education & training, program evaluation & improvement, and communication & coordination.   
   *“Every workplace should have a safety and health program that includes management leadership, worker participation, and a systematic approach to finding and fixing hazards. Regular workplace inspections are an important tool for identifying hazards and fixing them.”* [[1]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/319-osha_small_business_handbook.pdf#page=7)

2. **Conduct routine workplace self‑inspections** to identify hazards, control them, and verify that controls remain effective.   
   *“Small business employers should conduct routine workplace self‑inspections to: identify hazards, control identified hazards, and monitor and evaluate hazard controls to verify that they continue to be effective.”* [[2]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/319-osha_small_business_handbook.pdf#page=8)

3. **Use OSHA’s On‑Site Consultation Program** (no‑cost, confidential) to get expert help in spotting hazards, fixing them, and staying compliant.   
   *“The OSHA On‑Site Consultation Program offers no‑cost and confidential occupational safety and health services to small and medium‑sized businesses…”* [[3]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/319-osha_small_business_handbook.pdf#page=90)

4. **Provide appropriate training** for all workers on hazards that are specific to your work processes and for general safety and health topics.   
   *“OSHA’s education centers… deliver courses on OSHA standards and occupational safety and health topics to… private sector students.”* [[4]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/319-osha_small_business_handbook.pdf#page=92)

5. **Apply OSHA standards that are relevant to your business** (e.g., general industry 29 CFR 1910 for most small businesses).   
   *“OSHA has four separate sets of standards: General Industry (29 CFR 1910); Construction (29 CFR 1926); Maritime Employment (29 CFR 1915‑1919); Agriculture (29 CFR 1928).”* [[5]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/319-osha_small_business_handbook.pdf#page=91)

**Make your premises accessible**

1. **Identify and remove barriers** that prevent people with disabilities from accessing your business.   
   *“The ADA requires that newly constructed facilities … meet or exceed the minimum requirements of the ADA Standards for Accessible Design (Standards). Alterations to facilities… also must comply with the Standards.”* [[6]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/316-ada_guide_small_business.pdf#page=19)

2. **Ensure at least one entrance is accessible** (or provide an alternate accessible entrance).   
   *“When a business has two public entrances, in most cases, only one must be accessible.”* [[7]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/316-ada_guide_small_business.pdf#page=10)

3. **Provide accessible routes** such as ramps with a slope no greater than 1:12, handrails where the slope is steeper than 1:20 or the rise is >6 in., and a clearance of at least 36 in. width (42 in. preferred).

runs.question: how do i write a business plan and set up accounting
runs.answer:
To create a solid foundation for a new venture you can follow the step‑by‑step guidance found in the SBA Business Planning Guide and the IRS Publication 583 “Starting a Business.”  Both documents give clear, cited instructions on how to write a business plan and how to establish the accounting system that will support it.

---

## 1.  Writing a Business Plan  

1. **Begin with a clear outline** – The SBA guide lists the major sections you should include and gives an example order.  
   *Cover Page, Table of Contents (optional), Executive Summary, Business, Management, Market, Money, Exhibits*【sba_business_planning_guide.pdf, page 4】.

2. **Executive Summary** – Keep it brief (1–2 paragraphs). Describe your idea, the money you need, what you will do with the money, and a short schedule of goals. Write this last, because you will know the facts only after the rest of the plan is complete【sba_business_planning_guide.pdf, page 4】.

3. **Business Section** –  
   - Describe your product or service, its marketability, and how it will maintain a competitive advantage.  
   - Include any applicable regulations, licenses, and permits.  
   - Detail the facilities and equipment needed to operate the business.  
   See the guide for guidance on how to write each of these elements【sba_business_planning_guide.pdf, page 12】.

4. **Management Section** –  
   - Define ownership, the organizational structure, and responsibilities of key staff and outside consultants.  
   - Explain who will manage day‑to‑day operations, long‑term planning, and who monitors industry trends.  
   This section also invites you to list advisors and consultants that will provide the business with tax, legal, and financial advice【sba_business_planning_guide.pdf, page 13】.

5. **Market Section** –  
   - Identify the target market, competition, and how you will make and promote your product or service.  
   - Evaluate direct and indirect competitors, and explain how you will differentiate your business.  
   All of these steps are documented in the “Marketing” part of the guide【sba_business_planning_guide.pdf, page 14–15】.

6. **Money Section** – Provide financial documentation. The guide says you should include:  
   *Sources and uses of funds, 3‑year income projection, cash‑flow projection, notes and critical assumptions, and a break‑even analysis.  
   It also references balance sheets, personal financial statements, and tax returns you may need to show lenders【sba_business_planning_guide.pdf, page 16】.

7. **Exhibits** – Attach supporting documents such as resumes, purchase agreements, contracts, floor plans, licenses, and the financial statement packages you prepared【sba_business_planning_guide.pdf, page 4】.

8. **Finishing Touches** –  
   - Add a list of assumptions and supporting calculations in a separate “Notes and Critical Assumptions” page (use the guide’s worksheet as a template).  
   - Review the plan for accuracy and completeness before you share it with lenders, investors, or partners【sba_business_planning_guide.pdf, page 20】.

---

## 2.  Setting Up Accounting  

### 2.1 Pick a Business Structure & Obtain an EIN  
The IRS advises you to decide on the entity type (sole proprietorship, partnership, corporation, LLC, etc.) early on because it determines tax filing and accounting methods【irs_publication_583_starting_a_business.pdf, page 5】.  Once you have chosen, apply for an Employer Identification Number (EIN) – the IRS will issue this after you file the appropriate application.

### 2.2  Choose an Accounting Method  
The IRS explains how to select a method that shows your income clearly and consistently:

| Method | When it’s Generally Used | Key Feature |
|--------|--------------------------|-------------|
| **Cash** | No inventory, small business | Income is recorded when received; expenses when paid |
| **Accrual** | Inventory required or larger businesses | Income recorded when earned; expenses when incurred |
| **Special/Combination** | Certain situations | Mix of cash and accrual elements |

You decide on a method the first time you file a tax return that includes a Schedule C (Form 1040) for the business. If you later want to change the method, you typically need IRS approval via Form 1128【irs_publication_334_tax_guide_small_business.pdf, page 14】.

### 2.3  Keep Separate Books and Records  
“Keep a complete and separate set of books and records for each business.” 【irs_publication_583_starting_a_business.pdf, page 5】

### 2.4  Open a Business Checking Account  
The IRS publication recommends you open at least one business checking account “to keep your business account separate from your personal checking account.” It also suggests using a checkbook that gives you space to identify the source of each deposit and the type of expense【irs_publication_583_starting_a_business.pdf, page 14】.

### 2.5  Record Transactions Daily  
The guide says “record expenses when they occur, and identify the source of recorded receipts.”  “It is best to record transactions on a daily basis.” 【irs_publication_583_starting_a_business.pdf, page 14】

### 2.6  Reconcile Every Month  
Reconciling verifies that the bank statement, checkbook, and books agree.  You should “reconcile your checking account each month” and follow the steps for finding errors【irs_publication_583_starting_a_business.pdf, page 14】.

### 2.7  Deductible Business Expenses  
The IRS says an expense is deductible if it is “ordinary and necessary.”  Ordinary means “common and accepted in your field.” Needed means it is “helpful and appropriate for your business, trade, or profession.”  The publication lists specific expense categories that are commonly deductible (e.g., advertising, travel, supplies, etc.)【irs_publication_583_starting_a_business.pdf, page 9】.  It also notes that you can elect to deduct up to $5,000 of start‑up and organizational costs, with the remainder amortized【irs_publication_583_starting_a_business.pdf, page 9】.

runs.question: do i need an ein and what accounting method comes with it
runs.answer:
You only need an EIN (Employer Identification Number) if your business falls into a category that requires a separate federal taxpayer ID. The IRS lists the principal situations in the *Publication 583 – Starting a Business and Keeping Records* and in the *Publication 334 – Tax Guide for Small Businesses*:

- If you pay wages to one or more employees.  
  [[1]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/317-irs_publication_334_tax_guide_small_business.pdf#page=6)

- If you must file pension or excise‑tax returns.  
  [[1]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/317-irs_publication_334_tax_guide_small_business.pdf#page=6)

- And, in general, the IRS issues an EIN to sole proprietors, partnerships, corporations and other entities so that they can file returns and report income under a business TIN.  
  [[2]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/318-irs_publication_583_starting_a_business.pdf#page=4)

If none of those situations apply (e.g., you’re a sole proprietor who never hires employees and never files any of the special returns above), you could use your Social Security Number as your TIN instead of getting an EIN.

---

**Accounting Method**

When you file your first income‑tax return for the business, you must choose an accounting method. The method you “come with” is the one you select at that time, not anything that depends on whether you have an EIN. The publication says:

> “An accounting method is a set of rules used to determine when and how income and expenses are reported. You choose an accounting method for your business when you file your first income tax return.”  
  [[3]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/318-irs_publication_583_starting_a_business.pdf#page=5)

The two basic options are the **cash method** (report income when received, deduct expenses when paid) or the **accrual method** (report income when earned, deduct expenses when incurred). You can also use other special or combination methods, but the choice is made when you file your first return, not when you obtain an EIN.

runs.question: what accounting method should i use
runs.answer:
The IRS guidance says that the accounting method you pick depends mainly on whether your business holds inventory and on your size as a taxpayer.

**1. If you have no inventory**  
Most owners who do not keep inventory are advised to use the **cash method** because it is simpler: you record income when you receive it and expenses when you pay them – exactly the rule in the publications.

> *“Most individuals and many sole proprietors with no inventory use the cash method because they find it easier to keep cash‑method records.”* [[1]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/317-irs_publication_334_tax_guide_small_business.pdf#page=16)

**2. If you do hold inventory**  
When inventory is necessary to account for your income, the default is the **accrual method**. This is required unless you qualify as a small‑business taxpayer and can treat the inventory as non‑incidental material or supplies.

> *“If an inventory is necessary to account for your income, you must generally use an accrual method of accounting for sales and purchases unless you are a small business taxpayer (defined later in this chapter).”* [[1]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/317-irs_publication_334_tax_guide_small_business.pdf#page=16)

**3. Small‑business taxpayer definition**  
A small‑business taxpayer may use the cash method for inventory that is treated as non‑incidental materials or supplies:

> *“Small business taxpayer. You qualify as a small business taxpayer if you (a) have average annual gross receipts of $31 million or less for the 3 prior tax years (indexed for inflation), and (b) are not a tax shelter (as defined in section 448(d)(3)).”* [[1]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/317-irs_publication_334_tax_guide_small_business.pdf#page=16)

> *“Certain small business taxpayers can use the cash method of accounting and can also account for inventoriable items as materials and supplies that are not incidental.”* [[2]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/318-irs_publication_583_starting_a_business.pdf#page=5)

**Bottom line:**  

* Use the **cash method** if you **do not carry inventory**.  
* Use the **accrual method** if you carry inventory **and are not a qualifying small‑business taxpayer**.  
* If you **do** carry inventory **and qualify as a small‑business taxpayer**, you may treat the inventory as non‑incidental materials or supplies and still use the cash method.
