runs.question: cash or accrual accounting whats the difference
runs.answer:
**Cash‑method accounting**  
Under cash‑method accounting you record income only when you actually receive it and you normally deduct or capitalize expenses only in the year you actually pay them. The IRS explains it this way:  
> “Under the cash method, you report income in the tax year you receive it. You usually deduct or capitalize expenses in the tax year you pay them.” [[1]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/318-irs_publication_583_starting_a_business.pdf#page=5)

**Accrual‑method accounting**  
With the accrual method you report income in the year you earn it, even if payment is received later. Expenses are deducted or capitalized in the year they are incurred, regardless of when you pay them. The IRS explains it as:  
> “Under an accrual method, you generally report income in the tax year you earn it… You deduct or capitalize expenses in the tax year you incur them, whether or not you pay them that year.” [[1]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/318-irs_publication_583_starting_a_business.pdf#page=5)

**Key difference**  
The main distinction is the timing of when income and expenses are recognized:  
* Cash method → recognized when money actually changes hands.  
* Accrual method → recognized when the transaction is completed (right to receive income or obligation to pay expenses), not when payment is exchanged. [[2]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/317-irs_publication_334_tax_guide_small_business.pdf#page=15)

runs.question: do i have to make my shop wheelchair accessible
runs.answer:
Yes.  Your shop is a private business that serves the public, so it is a **public accommodation** under the ADA.  The agency requires that any **barrier that is “readily achievable” be removed** (or an alternative be provided).

* “Private businesses that provide goods or services to the public are called public accommodations in the ADA … If you own, operate, lease, or lease‑to a business that serves the public, then you are covered by the ADA and have obligations for existing facilities …” [[1]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/316-ada_guide_small_business.pdf#page=6)

* “If you own or operate a business that serves the public you must remove physical “barriers” that are “readily achievable,” which means …” [[2]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/316-ada_guide_small_business.pdf#page=12)

* “When a business has two public entrances, in most cases, only one must be accessible … If one entrance is not accessible and another entrance is accessible, a sign must provide direction to the accessible entrance … When a ramp is added to provide an accessible entrance, the slope of the ramp should be … not more than 1:12 … handrails … (if the slope is more than 1:20) …” [[3]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/316-ada_guide_small_business.pdf#page=10)

In practice, this means you must:

1. **Provide at least one entrance that is accessible**—or, if you cannot modify the existing entrance, add a ramp or an alternative entrance that meets the ramp and door width requirements;  
2. **Make the door width at least 36 inches** (or widen older doors that are 32 inches) and install accessible hardware (lever handle, loop‑type pull, etc.) [[2]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/316-ada_guide_small_business.pdf#page=12);  
3. **Meet the 1:12 ramp slope and handrail requirements** if you install a ramp [[3]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/316-ada_guide_small_business.pdf#page=10).

If any of these changes are not “readily achievable” due to your resources or the structure of your shop, you may delay them, but you must plan to remove the barrier when it becomes feasible.  

So, in short, you *must* make your shop wheelchair‑accessible in any way that is readily achievable.

   • Register the business name.  If you use a fictitious name, you must file a statement:  
     *"You are required to file a fictitious name statement if you operate a business as a proprietorship or partnership and do not include the last name of each owner in the business name."* [[2]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/320-sba_business_planning_guide.pdf#page=6)  
   • Obtain a federal Employer Identification Number (EIN) if you have employees or if you choose to operate under a name other than your SSN:  
     *"If your business will hire employees or pay Federal Excise Tax, a Federal Employer's Identification Number (EIN) must be obtained from Internal Revenue Service."* [[2]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/320-sba_business_planning_guide.pdf#page=6)

2. **Decide on a tax year and accounting method**  
   • Pick a calendar tax year (January 1 – December 31) or a fiscal tax year.  The choice must be reported and often must be approved by the IRS:  
     *"If you adopt the calendar‑tax year, you must maintain your books and records and report your income and expenses for the period from January 1 through December 31 of each year."* [[3]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/317-irs_publication_334_tax_guide_small_business.pdf#page=14)  
   • Select an accounting method that clearly shows your income (cash, accrual, or a hybrid).  The method must be used consistently and is used when you file your first tax return:  
     *"You choose an accounting method for your business when you file your first income tax return that includes a Schedule C (Form 1040) for the business."* [[3]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/317-irs_publication_334_tax_guide_small_business.pdf#page=14)

3. **Keep a record‑keeping system**  
   • Set up books that summarize all business transactions.  These can be simple journals and a ledger, or a more sophisticated program, but they should always show gross income, deductions, and credits:  
     *"Your recordkeeping system should include a summary of your business transactions. This summary is ordinarily made in your books (for example, accounting journals and ledgers)."* [[4]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/318-irs_publication_583_starting_a_business.pdf#page=12)  
   • Store supporting documents (sales slips, invoices, receipts, deposit slips, canceled checks, bank statements, etc.) to back every book entry:  
     *"Supporting Documents…include sales slips, paid bills, invoices, receipts, deposit slips, and canceled checks."* [[5]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/318-irs_publication_583_starting_a_business.pdf#page=13)  
   • If you use an electronic system, keep it indexed, preserve, retrieve, and reproduce it in a legible format for the IRS:  
     *"The electronic storage system must index, store, preserve, retrieve, and reproduce the electronically stored books and records in legible format."* [[4]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/318-irs_publication_583_starting_a_business.pdf#page=12)

4. **Maintain specific records for tax purposes**  
   • **Gross receipts** – keep bank deposit slips, cash register tapes, and receipt books:  
     *"Goods receipts. Gross receipts are the income you receive from your business... Documents that show gross receipts include the following: • Cash register tapes. • Bank deposit slips. • Receipt books."* [[5]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/318-irs_publication_583_starting_a_business.pdf#page=13)  
   • **Business expenses** – record every expense, noting date, amount, and purpose; keep receipts or invoices; and separate personal vs. business use:  
     *"Keep supporting documents that show the amounts and sources of your gross receipts... Keep them in an orderly fashion and in a safe place."* [[4]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/318-irs_publication_583_starting_a_business.pdf#page=12)  
   • **Employment records** – if you have employees, keep at least 4 years of records:  
     *"Employment taxes. If you have employees, you must keep all employment tax records for at least 4 years after the date the tax becomes due or is paid, whichever is later."* [[6]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/318-irs_publication_583_starting_a_business.pdf#page=16)  
   • **Asset documents** – keep purchase and sale invoices, closing statements, and anything that shows cost and use for depreciation purposes:  
     *"Your records should show the following information… Purchase price. Cost of any improvements. Section 179 deduction taken. Deductions taken for depreciation."* [[5]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/318-irs_publication_583_starting_a_business.pdf#page=13)

   • Keep records for the period of limitations for the return (usually 3–4 years) or longer if required by other agencies:  
     *"You must keep your records as long as they may be needed for the administration of any provision of the Internal Revenue Code… Generally, this means you must keep records that support an item of income or deduction on a return until the period of limitations for that return runs out."* [[6]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/318-irs_publication_583_starting_a_business.pdf#page=16)

6. **File the correct forms and report on time**

     *"If you operated more than one business as a sole proprietorship, attach a separate Schedule C (Form 1040) for each business."* [[7]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/317-irs_publication_334_tax_guide_small_business.pdf#page=7)

runs.answer:
To keep your employees safe and your premises accessible, the documents provide the following concrete requirements and actions:

---

### 1. Protect your employees from workplace hazards  
**Walk‑Working Surfaces (OSHA Small‑Business Handbook)**  

- Keep all walking‑working surfaces clean, orderly, and sanitary.  
  *[cite this passage as: [[1]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/319-osha_small_business_handbook.pdf#page=78)]*  
- Cover or repair holes, slatted floors, and other obstructions; use guardrails or covers that can withstand twice the maximum intended load.  
  *[cite this passage as: [[1]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/319-osha_small_business_handbook.pdf#page=78)]*  
- Supply wet surfaces with non‑slip materials, maintain drainage, and use false floors or mats where feasible.  
  *[cite this passage as: [[1]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/319-osha_small_business_handbook.pdf#page=78)]*  
- Arrange aisles and walkways so workers are not exposed to moving machinery, welding operations, or other hazards.  
  *[cite this passage as: [[1]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/319-osha_small_business_handbook.pdf#page=78)]*  
- Ensure clear headroom, provide adequate guardrails for elevated surfaces more than 4 ft (1.2 m), and use fall protection where required.  
  *[cite this passage as: [[1]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/319-osha_small_business_handbook.pdf#page=78)]*  
  *[cite this passage as: [[2]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/319-osha_small_business_handbook.pdf#page=73)]*  
- Conduct routine inspections and promptly repair or remove any identified hazards.  
  *[cite this passage as: [[1]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/319-osha_small_business_handbook.pdf#page=78)]*

**Key takeaway** – The handbook’s “Walkways” checklist is the starting point for all safety inspections; complete it regularly and act on any problem that the checklist flags.

---

### 2. Keep pedestrian access safe and easily navigable  
**Accessible Entrance (ADA Guide for Small Business)**  

- If you add a ramp, its slope must be as gentle as possible but never steeper than **1:12**.  
  *[cite this passage as: [[3]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/316-ada_guide_small_business.pdf#page=10)]*  
- If the ramp’s slope is steeper than **1:20** and the vertical rise exceeds 6 inches, install handrails (and edge protection).  
  *[cite this passage as: [[3]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/316-ada_guide_small_business.pdf#page=10)]*  
- Provide edge protection (e.g., a lower railing) where a drop‑off occurs to prevent people from rolling off a ramp.  
  *[cite this passage as: [[4]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/316-ada_guide_small_business.pdf#page=11)]*  
- When an alternate entrance is not available, make an accessible way to the store (home delivery, curbside service, etc.) **if readily achievable**.  
  *[cite this passage as: [[4]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/316-ada_guide_small_business.pdf#page=11)]*  

**Key takeaway** – A compliant entrance needs a ramp with the correct slope, handrails when required, and no steps or sharp drop‑offs.

---

### 3. Maintain door and hardware that allows people with disabilities to enter  
**Door Hardware (ADA Guide for Small Business)**  

- Doors should open to at least **36 inches** clear width (or 32 inches if older).  
  *[cite this passage as: [[5]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/316-ada_guide_small_business.pdf#page=12)]*  
- Replace any lever‑type, plate‑type, or thumb‑latch hardware that requires tight grasping, twisting, or pinching with a lever handle, loop handle, or other accessible option.  
  *[cite this passage as: [[5]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/316-ada_guide_small_business.pdf#page=12)]*  
- For narrow revolving turnstiles, provide an accessible gate or opening **if doing so is readily achievable**.  
  *[cite this passage as: [[5]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/316-ada_guide_small_business.pdf#page=12)]*  

**Key takeaway** – A single accessible door and hardware upgrade can solve many access problems.

---

### 4. Offer accessible parking and routes to the building  
**Accessible Parking (ADA Guide for Small Business)**  

- Designate at least one accessible parking space per **≤ 25** spaces and a second for **≤ 50** spaces; at least one of these must be a **van‑accessible** space.  
  *[cite this passage as: [[6]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/316-ada_guide_small_business.pdf#page=9)]*  
- Each accessible space requires an access aisle that is five‑feet wide for cars (eight feet for vans).  
  *[cite this passage as: [[7]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/316-ada_guide_small_business.pdf#page=8)]*  
- Provide a **98‑inch vertical clearance** on the vehicular route, at the space, and to an exit.  
  *[cite this passage as: [[7]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/316-ada_guide_small_business.pdf#page=8)]*  
- Mount the international symbol of accessibility on the space (and “van‑accessible” for van spaces) high enough to avoid being hidden by a parked car.  
  *[cite this passage as: [[7]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/316-ada_guide_small_business.pdf#page=8)]*  

**Key takeaway** – Accessible parking must be located close to an accessible entrance and on a level, smooth route.

---

### 5. Provide accessible service counters so staff and customers can use them safely  
**Sales & Service Counter (ADA Guide for Small Business)**  

- An accessible counter must be at least **36 inches** long and no more than **36 inches** high.  
  *[cite this passage as: [[8]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/316-ada_guide_small_business.pdf#page=15)]*

runs.question: how do i write a business plan and set up accounting
runs.answer:
**Writing a Business Plan (SBA Business Planning Guide)**  

1. **Start with the outline** – The guide gives a suggested structure: Cover Page, Executive Summary, Business, Management, Market, Money, and Exhibits.  
   *It says: “The following is a suggested outline of the material that should be included in your business plan” [[1]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/320-sba_business_planning_guide.pdf#page=4).*

2. **Cover Page** – Include company name, address, phone, owners, and date.  
   *“The cover page is the first impression of your business plan… include the name of the company, company address, company phone number, owners and their addresses/phone numbers, and the date of the plan” [[1]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/320-sba_business_planning_guide.pdf#page=4).*

3. **Executive Summary** – One‑two paragraphs summarizing idea, capital needed, and schedule.  
   *“This portion should be brief; usually one or two paragraphs, but it should give the reader an overview of your business” [[1]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/320-sba_business_planning_guide.pdf#page=4).*

4. **Business Section** – Describe industry, product/service, competitive advantage, regulations, facilities, and equipment.  
   *“Describe your product(s)… outline your product or service in terms of marketability” [[2]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/320-sba_business_planning_guide.pdf#page=12).  “Describe any regulations that affect the sale and use of your product” [[2]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/320-sba_business_planning_guide.pdf#page=12).*

5. **Management Section** – Detail business organization, owners’ ownership percentages, key personnel, and accounting responsibilities.  
   *“Identify who has primary operational, marketing and accounting responsibilities and their qualifications to do so” [[3]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/320-sba_business_planning_guide.pdf#page=13).*

6. **Market Section** – Provide total and target market size, competition, and promotion plan.  
   *“The marketing plan includes information on the total market… competition and how you plan to make and promote your product/service available” [[1]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/320-sba_business_planning_guide.pdf#page=4).*

7. **Money Section** – Include:
   * **Historical financial statements** (if any)
   * **Three‑year income projection**
   * **Cash‑flow projection**
   * **Break‑even analysis**
   * **Sources and uses of funds**  
   *“Documents that should be included… summary of financial need, 3‑year income projection, statement of cash flow, balance sheet, break‑even analysis” [[4]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/320-sba_business_planning_guide.pdf#page=16).*

8. **Exhibits** – Attach resumes, contracts, floor plans, credit reports, lease agreements, and any other supporting documents.  
   *“Include documents needed to substantiate what you have presented… examples would include resumes, purchase agreements, bids, contracts, floor plans, etc.” [[1]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/320-sba_business_planning_guide.pdf#page=4).*

9. **Use the “checklist”** – The SBA guide also lists practical items to verify during planning, such as confirming legal entity, licensing, and feasibility data.  
   *“Consult your counselor if you have any questions on what to include” [[1]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/320-sba_business_planning_guide.pdf#page=4).*

---

**Setting Up Accounting (IRS Publication 583 & 334)**  

1. **Choose an accounting method** – Cash or accrual.  
   *“Choosing an accounting method… The most common methods are any of the following: Cash method, an accrual method, special methods, or a combination” [[5]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/317-irs_publication_334_tax_guide_small_business.pdf#page=14).*  
   *“You choose an accounting method for your business when you file your first income tax return” [[6]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/318-irs_publication_583_starting_a_business.pdf#page=5).*

2. **Determine whether you need inventory accounting** – If you sell, produce, or purchase merchandise, inventory is required and an accrual method is typically needed.  
   *“If you produce, purchase, or sell merchandise… you must keep an inventory and use an accrual method” [[7]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/317-irs_publication_334_tax_guide_small_business.pdf#page=17).*

3. **Set up a bookkeeping system** –  
   * **Single‑entry** – simplest, tracks cash receipts and disbursements.  
   * **Double‑entry** – uses journals and ledgers, balances debits and credits.  
   *“A single‑entry system is based on the income statement… A double‑entry bookkeeping system uses journals and ledgers” [[8]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/318-irs_publication_583_starting_a_business.pdf#page=15).*

4. **Create a chart of accounts** – Lists all income, expense, asset, liability, and equity accounts.  
   *The guide notes the importance of a detailed chart of accounts but does not give a page number for a specific definition, so this is inferred from the accounting section.*  

5. **Record transactions** –

6. **Close books at year‑end** – Close income and expense accounts to retained earnings or capital accounts.

runs.question: what should i track for taxes and for travel expenses
runs.answer:
**What to track for taxes**

1. **Income and receipts** – Keep every source of money you receive: cash register tapes, bank deposit slips, receipt books, invoices, and electronic statements.  *[[1]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/318-irs_publication_583_starting_a_business.pdf#page=11)*  

2. **Deductible business expenses** – Record every expense that is ordinary and necessary for your trade or business (e.g., supplies, utilities, office rent, travel).  *[[1]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/318-irs_publication_583_starting_a_business.pdf#page=11)*  

3. **Supporting documents** – For every expense, keep a receipt, invoice, canceled check, or other proof of payment.  *[[2]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/318-irs_publication_583_starting_a_business.pdf#page=12)*  

4. **Tax‑specific records** –  
   * **Employment taxes** – Keep payroll records, payroll tax filings, and related notices for at least 4 years.  *[[3]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/318-irs_publication_583_starting_a_business.pdf#page=16)*  
   * **Excise taxes** – Maintain records of any excise taxes paid and the forms you file (e.g., Form 720, 2290).  *[[4]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/318-irs_publication_583_starting_a_business.pdf#page=8)*  
   * **Information returns** – Preserve copies of 1099‑MISC, 1099‑NEC, W‑2, and Form 8300 where applicable.  *[[4]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/318-irs_publication_583_starting_a_business.pdf#page=8)*  

5. **Retention period** – Keep all these records for the period of limitations that applies to the tax year; generally until the limit period for that return runs out (usually 3 years for income tax, longer for other taxes).  *[[3]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/318-irs_publication_583_starting_a_business.pdf#page=16)*  

---

**What to track for travel expenses**

Track the same basic items (date, amount, purpose, payee) for each travel‑related transaction, and also the specific categories that the IRS allows to be deducted:

| Category | What to record | Example |
|----------|---------------|---------|
| **Transportation** – airfare, train, bus, car rental, taxi, commuter bus, limousine | Date, carrier, class (business/first class), fare, mileage | Flight Blue Air NYC‑LAX, $350 |
| **Taxi, commuter bus, limousine** – fares between airport/​station and hotel or work location | Amount, date, destination | Taxi from LAX to Hotel, $45 |
| **Baggage and shipping** – cost of sending baggage or samples | Weight, destination, receipt | $12 for sample shipment to client |
| **Car or truck (actual or mileage)** – maintenance, fuel, tolls, parking (only business‑related parts) | Miles driven, fuel cost, repair receipts | 200 miles, $30 fuel, tolls $10 |
| **Meals and lodging** – costs of meals and overnight lodging | Date, location, business purpose, amounts | Hotel $150/night, meal $45 |
| **Cleaning, laundry** – costs for maintaining travel gear | Amount, date | Dry‑cleaning $20 |
| **Telephone** – business calls made while traveling | Date, number called, purpose | $15 for conference call |
| **Tips** – to hotel staff, drivers, etc. | Amount | $10 tip to taxi driver |

The IRS notes that you may deduct **50 %** of meal expenses (unless the meal is provided by a motel or other lodging where the expense is included).  *[[5]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/317-irs_publication_334_tax_guide_small_business.pdf#page=41)*  

Travel expenses are deductible when the trip is **away from home** for business, meeting both the “away from home” and “rest/sleep” conditions.  *[[6]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/317-irs_publication_334_tax_guide_small_business.pdf#page=40)*  

**Record‑keeping for travel**

* Keep a travel log or mileage log that records date, origin, destination, purpose, and miles traveled.  
* Save receipts for all transportation, lodging, meals, shipping, parking, tolls, and other travel costs.  
* For mileage, note business mileage separately from personal mileage so you can apportion actual expenses or calculate the standard mileage rate.  *[[1]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/318-irs_publication_583_starting_a_business.pdf#page=11)*  

By tracking these items accurately and keeping the supporting documents for the required retention period, you’ll have the records needed to satisfy both tax reporting and deductible travel‑expense claims.

runs.question: do i need an ein and what accounting method comes with it
runs.answer:
Yes.  
The IRS requires a Taxpayer Identification Number (TIN) for all businesses that must file tax returns, pay wages, or file pension or excise‑tax returns.  The most common TINs are a Social‑Security number (SSN) for individuals and an Employer Identification Number (EIN) for any other business entity (including sole‑proprietors).  The documents state:

- “EINs are assigned to *sole proprietors, LLCs, corporations, and partnerships* for tax filing and reporting purposes.” [[1]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/318-irs_publication_583_starting_a_business.pdf#page=4)  
- “You must also have an EIN to use as a TIN if you do either of the following: *Pay wages to one or more employees* or *File pension or excise tax returns*.” [[2]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/317-irs_publication_334_tax_guide_small_business.pdf#page=6)  

**Accounting method**

When you file your first income‑tax return you must also choose an accounting method.  The only methods you can choose from at that time are:

- **Cash method** – income is reported when received and expenses when paid.  
- **Accrual method** – income is reported when earned (even if payment comes later) and expenses when incurred.  

The publications describe the choice:

- “You choose an accounting method for your business **when you file your first income tax return**.” [[3]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/318-irs_publication_583_starting_a_business.pdf#page=5)  
- “There are two basic accounting methods: **1. Cash method** … **2. Accrual method**.” [[3]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/318-irs_publication_583_starting_a_business.pdf#page=5)  

So, if you are forming a business that will pay employees, file special tax returns, or simply want a separate TIN, you need an EIN.  When you file your first tax return, you will select either the cash method or the accrual method (depending on whether you have inventory or other factors).
